overview: The Apsáalooke, often called Crow, are a living Northern Plains people with a homeland in and around present-day Montana. Their history includes seasonal bison hunting, three major bands, extensive family relationships and the preservation of language and community life through profound changes in landholding and government.

periods.title: Horses transform movement and hunting
periods.summary: Little Big Horn College places the acquisition of horses around 1725. Greater carrying capacity and mobility changed hunting, travel and the scale of movable dwellings.

periods.title: History carried on a painted robe
periods.summary: A surviving bison-hide robe, dated approximately 1850 by the National Museum of the American Indian, records its owner’s accomplishments in pictorial scenes.

periods.title: A treaty defines a reservation
periods.summary: The treaty signed at Fort Laramie on 7 May 1868 defined reserved lands and required the cession of other territorial claims. It also included conditional hunting provisions outside the reservation.

periods.title: A difficult transition to reservation life
periods.summary: With bison no longer sustaining the earlier economy, cattle distributions helped households survive. Government policies pressed people toward new livelihoods, schooling arrangements and settlement patterns.

periods.title: A constitution describes divided powers
periods.summary: The Crow government identifies its 2001 Constitution as the basis for separate executive, legislative and judicial branches, with checks and balances among them.

periods.title: Community researchers work with museum collections
periods.summary: Apsáalooke visitors studied historic beadwork, bows, films and recordings at the Smithsonian, connecting older material and recorded knowledge with contemporary teaching.

items.text: Smaller winter villages could come together in the warmer part of the year, when the major bands gathered and hunted. Dried meat, roots and berries helped sustain households in winter. Food preservation mattered alongside the hunt: the ability to store and share provisions supported community life through seasons with very different opportunities.

Matrilineal clans and an extended network of relatives shaped responsibility for children. A mother’s sisters were also mothers, and a father’s brothers were also fathers in the kinship system described by the college. These relationships made care and belonging broader than the small household model familiar to many outsiders.

Horses increased the loads families could move and the distances hunters could cover. Larger tipi loads became practical as transport changed. The approximate early eighteenth-century adoption date describes a transformation in an existing society, not its beginning; horse expertise was developed through learning, use and exchange.

The NMAI’s robe 1/2558 combines bison hide, pigment, trade cloth, beads and porcupine quillwork. Its approximately 1850 date is a museum attribution; acquisition at Fort Benton in 1861 is a separate event. Bringing different materials together required hide preparation, painting and decorative skills, and also reflects access to traded goods.

Apsáalooke historian Patrick J. Hill and Timothy P. McCleary interpret the robe’s six scenes as a public account of martial accomplishments. They explain its pictorial conventions as narrative writing. The object is therefore evidence of a way to communicate remembered deeds, rather than merely an ornamental surface.

Tipi liner 18/9242 preserves cotton canvas, deer hooves, glass beads and porcupine quills, with bead stitching and quill wrapping recorded in its catalogue. The museum bought it from a New York dealer in 1936. Its maker, manufacture date and earlier ownership are not supplied, so that purchase cannot be presented as an excavation or a date of invention.

Liners helped manage drafts, dampness and ventilation inside tipis. During the reservation period, some families carried their use into log houses. Crow house interiors could retain a central stove, an east-facing entrance and decorated wall linings. New construction materials did not automatically erase established ways of organizing domestic space.

The 1868 treaty made a reservation the prescribed permanent home while retaining specified hunting rights on unoccupied United States land, subject to conditions in its text. Reading both provisions matters: reservation boundaries did not by themselves describe every place the agreement allowed Crow people to use. These are the treaty’s historical terms.

Boarding schools separated children from their families as part of federal assimilation policy. Families established camps near reservation missions, keeping themselves closer to children attending those schools. This response shows parents working within severe constraints to preserve relationships; attendance cannot be read simply as willing abandonment of Crow social life.

Plenty Coups’ preserved homestead near Pryor includes a log house, farm and store. Montana’s state park account dates his residence there from 1884 until his death in 1932. The buildings provide concrete evidence of a leader negotiating new economic conditions through farming and commerce, alongside his public responsibilities.

Crow Fair brings people together in a large gathering that includes a tipi encampment and public cultural activities. In the college’s account it belongs to continuing social life, alongside smaller family and community relationships. A historical card should place such gatherings in the present as well as discuss nineteenth-century objects.

In March 2016, Apsáalooke researchers at the Smithsonian examined beadwork and horn-reinforced bows, documenting construction for possible recreation and teaching. They treated museum holdings as resources for living knowledge. The project’s proposed digital archive was a goal described at the time, not a product whose completion this account establishes.

The same visitors viewed a film of the 1908 Crow Fair and listened to later commentary recorded by Dean Bear Claw. Their own explanations added another layer of knowledge. This work connects community interpretation with museum records; collecting an old film alone does not preserve all the meanings that knowledgeable viewers can recognize.

The tribe’s official website describes executive, legislative and judicial branches under its 2001 Constitution. Tribal government is a continuing institution, with public responsibilities extending beyond cultural representation. Its existence makes it particularly misleading to treat the final year of an imported historical map polygon as the disappearance of a people.

ending.text: The Apsáalooke continue as a people and a self-governing tribe. Treaties and reservation policies profoundly restricted land and reshaped institutions, but did not end their community. The imported 1492 to 1500 map interval is not their historical lifetime or an extinction date.
